title: Response-Adaptive Randomization: Promise and Pitfalls

slides.heading: Shifting Probabilities Mid-Trial
slides.body: Response-adaptive randomization allows changing the allocation probability during the study by using the data accruing as the study progresses based on patient responses.
slides.image_prompt: an arrow pointing dynamically upward on a probability gauge next to medical charts

slides.heading: The Play-the-Winner Rule
slides.body: An example of response-adaptive randomization is the randomized play-the-winner rule. If a patient response is success, the next patient will be allocated to the same treatment group.
slides.image_prompt: two pill bottles where one bottle receives more tokens based on previous success tokens

slides.heading: Ethical Appeal vs Practical Limits
slides.body: This method is based on the ethics of allowing more patients to be allocated to treatments that benefit the patients. However, if clinical studies take a very long time to obtain results, this method cannot be recommended.
slides.image_prompt: a hourglass standing next to a clinical trial dossier and a row of patient figures

takeaway: Response-adaptive designs allocate more patients to winning treatments but fail if outcome feedback is slow.
references: Lim, C.-Y., & In, J. (2019). Randomization in clinical studies. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 72(3), 221-232.
caption: Response-adaptive randomization aligns trial design with patient benefit by shifting allocation probabilities toward successful treatments as data accumulates. However, if your trial requires lengthy follow-ups to evaluate responses, this approach becomes impractical. What is your perspective on ethical adaptive designs versus traditional fixed allocation?

title: The Ethical Dilemma of Randomization in Research

slides.heading: Probability Versus Physician Choice
slides.body: An ethical debate needs to examine whether the treatment method for subjects should be determined by probability rather than by the physician.
slides.image_prompt: a doctor holding a coin over a patient chart while standing at a hospital desk

slides.heading: The Burden on Participants
slides.body: Furthermore, the subjects may be given a placebo, and not treatment. Some subjects have to undergo further treatment, representing the cost that society has to pay for the benefit of future subjects.
slides.image_prompt: a patient figure standing at a crossroads holding a document and a sealed envelope

slides.heading: Individual vs Collective Ethics
slides.body: This ethical dilemma on the balance between individual ethics and collective ethics is still spawning much controversy.
slides.image_prompt: two balance scales held by hands, with one side showing an individual and the other showing a crowd

takeaway: Clinical trials force individual participants to accept risks and uncertainties so that future patients may benefit.
references: Lim, C.-Y., & In, J. (2019). Randomization in clinical studies. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 72(3), 221-232.
caption: Randomization is essential for scientific objectivity and causal inference, but it creates a deep ethical friction between individual care and collective medical progress. Patients may receive placebos or suboptimal treatments purely by chance, bearing a social cost for future generations. How do you address this fundamental tension during informed consent discussions?

title: Why PICO Fails Non-Intervention Questions

slides.heading: Origins in Epidemiology
slides.body: The PICO mnemonic was originally developed from an epidemiological perspective for medical intervention or exposure questions comparing one treatment over another.
slides.image_prompt: two distinct pill bottles sitting side by side on a table with a directional arrow pointing from one to the other

slides.heading: Built for Which Questions
slides.body: PICO is most suitable for which type questions that compare one treatment, therapy, or intervention over another, but lacks usefulness for diagnosis and prognosis.
slides.image_prompt: a researcher holding a scale balancing two different medical documents representing a comparison between options
slides.highlight: most suitable for which type questions

slides.heading: Beyond the Medical Model
slides.body: Nursing practice is routinely concerned with questions of what, when, how, and why, which often lie outside a strict medical model of cure or therapy.
slides.image_prompt: a simple figure surrounded by question mark symbols of different sizes pointing in various directions

slides.heading: The Qualitative Blind Spot
slides.body: Despite adaptations like removing the comparator, PICO remains ill-suited for identifying qualitative research articles focused on process and meaning.
slides.image_prompt: an open journal page displaying a person icon and a speech bubble symbol next to a magnifying glass

takeaway: PICO is tailored for intervention comparisons and struggles with qualitative, diagnostic, or descriptive inquiries.
references: Booth, A., O’Rourke, A. J., & Ford, N. J. (2000). Structuring the pre-search reference interview: a useful technique for handling clinical questions.
Huang, X., Lin, J., & Demner-Fushman, D. (2006). Evaluation of PICO as a knowledge representation for clinical questions.
Ou, C. H. K., Hall, W. A., & Thorne, S. E. (2017). Can nursing epistemology embrace p‐values?. Nursing Philosophy, 18(4). https://doi.org/10.1111/nup.12173
Cooke, A., Smith, D., & Booth, A. (2012). Beyond PICO. Qualitative Health Research, 22(10), 1435–1443. https://doi.org/10.1177/1049732312452938
caption: When your research question is about patient experience, meaning, or complex care processes, forcing it into a PICO framework can be like trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. Because it was built for comparative intervention trials, it leaves out vital dimensions of clinical inquiry. How do you structure your searches for qualitative or descriptive topics?

title: Why Content Validity Comes First in PROM Reviews

slides.heading: The Core of PROM Quality
slides.body: Content validity refers to the degree to which the content of a PROM is an adequate reflection of the construct to be measured.
slides.image_prompt: a magnifying glass held over a structured document filled with checkmarks, revealing a clear core concept highlighted in bright ink

slides.heading: Why It Ranks First
slides.body: Content validity is considered to be the most important measurement property because items must be relevant, comprehensive, and comprehensible.
slides.image_prompt: a researcher balancing a stack of heavy survey documents on one hand while pointing at a foundational bedrock block at the base

slides.heading: The Stop Rule for Bad Content
slides.body: If there is high quality evidence that the content validity is insufficient, the PROM will not be considered further in steps six to eight.
slides.image_prompt: a large red stop sign blocking a pathway of stacked papers, forcing a simple figure to turn in a different direction

takeaway: Content validity is the primary check in reviewing PROMs; if it fails, further evaluation stops.
references: Mokkink, L. B., Terwee, C. B., Patrick, D. L., Alonso, J., Stratford, P. W., Knol, D. L., Bouter, L. M., & de Vet, H. C. (2010). The COSMIN study reached international consensus on taxonomy, terminology, and definitions of measurement properties for health-related patient-reported outcomes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 63(7), 737–745. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2010.02.006

Prinsen, C. A. C., Mokkink, L. B., Bouter, L. M., Alonso, J., Patrick, D. L., de Vet, H. C. W., & Terwee, C. B. (2018). COSMIN guideline for systematic reviews of patient-reported outcome measures. Quality of Life Research, 27(1147–1157).
caption: When conducting a systematic review of patient-reported outcome measures, not all steps carry equal weight. Content validity acts as the absolute gatekeeper. If an instrument fails to capture the construct properly, testing its internal structure or reliability is a waste of time. How do you weight content validity in your current review protocols?

title: Reflective vs. Formative Models in Scale Testing

slides.heading: Understanding Reflective Models
slides.body: A reflective model assumes that all items in a scale are manifestations of one underlying construct and are expected to be correlated.
slides.image_prompt: a central glowing core connected by multiple dotted lines to several identical smaller glowing spheres floating around it

slides.heading: The Example of Anxiety
slides.body: Anxiety manifests itself in specific characteristics such as worrying thoughts, panic, and restlessness, reflecting the core construct.
slides.image_prompt: a simple figure surrounded by small floating icons representing different symptoms all pointing inward toward the person

slides.heading: When Step Six Does Not Apply
slides.body: If items in a scale are not supposed to be correlated, known as a formative model, internal structure analyses are not relevant.
slides.image_prompt: a researcher sorting separate building blocks into distinct independent piles rather than connecting them into a single tower

takeaway: Internal structure tests only apply to reflective models where items reflect an underlying construct.
references: de Vet, H. C., Terwee, C. B., Mokkink, L. B., & Knol, D. L. (2011). Measurement in medicine. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Prinsen, C. A. C., Mokkink, L. B., Bouter, L. M., Alonso, J., Patrick, D. L., de Vet, H. C. W., & Terwee, C. B. (2018). COSMIN guideline for systematic reviews of patient-reported outcome measures. Quality of Life Research, 27(5), 1147–1157. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11136-018-1798-3
caption: Before running factor analyses or checking internal consistency, you must identify whether your scale is reflective or formative. Applying classical psychometric tests to a formative index will yield misleading conclusions. Does your instrument treat items as causes or manifestations?

title: Why Structural Validity Must Precede Internal Consistency

slides.heading: The Sequence of Psychometric Testing
slides.body: A proven scale or subscale structure is a prerequisite for the proper interpretation of internal consistency analyses like Cronbach alpha.
slides.image_prompt: a builder carefully placing a solid foundation block on the ground before stacking upper levels of a building

slides.heading: Evaluating Structural Validity
slides.body: Structural validity refers to the degree to which scores reflect the dimensionality of the construct, usually assessed via factor analysis.
slides.image_prompt: a magnifying glass focused on a complex web of intersecting lines being sorted into clean parallel columns

slides.heading: Unidimensionality and Subscales
slides.body: Multiple factor analyses assess whether each subscale on its own measures a single construct before calculating internal consistency.
slides.image_prompt: a large group of mixed shapes being separated into distinct uniform boxes by a series of dividers

takeaway: Never calculate Cronbach alpha before confirming that the scale is actually unidimensional.
references: Mokkink, L. B., Terwee, C. B., Patrick, D. L., Alonso, J., Stratford, P. W., Knol, D. L., et al. (2010). The COSMIN study reached international consensus on taxonomy, terminology, and definitions of measurement properties for health-related patient-reported outcomes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 63(7), 737–745.

Prinsen, C. A. C., Mokkink, L. B., Bouter, L. M., Alonso, J., Patrick, D. L., de Vet, H. C. W., & Terwee, C. B. (2018). COSMIN guideline for systematic reviews of patient-reported outcome measures. Quality of Life Research, 27(1147–1157).
caption: Calculating Cronbach alpha on a multidimensional scale is a common methodological trap. Internal consistency assumes unidimensionality. If your factor structure is flawed, your alpha value is meaningless. How often do you check structural validity before diving into reliability coefficients?

title: Critical Appraisal vs. Reporting Guidelines: Know the Difference

slides.heading: Two Distinct Sets of Tools
slides.body: Nurses engaged in evidence-based practice have two important sets of tools: critical appraisal tools and reporting guidelines.
slides.image_prompt: a researcher standing between two large filing cabinets, one labeled with a checkmark and the other with a magnifying glass

slides.heading: Evaluating with Critical Appraisal Tools
slides.body: Critical appraisal tools facilitate the appraisal process and guide a consumer of evidence through an objective, analytical, evaluation process.
slides.image_prompt: a magnifying glass held over a stack of scientific documents on a wooden table, revealing clean grid lines

slides.heading: Ensuring Clarity with Reporting Guidelines
slides.body: Reporting guidelines are checklists of items that should be included in a publication to ensure clarity, completeness, and transparency.
slides.image_prompt: a person checking items off a large clipboard using a marker while looking at a completed manuscript

takeaway: Critical appraisal evaluates evidence quality, while reporting guidelines ensure transparent dissemination of findings.
references: Buccheri, R. K., & Sharifi, C. (2017). Critical Appraisal Tools and Reporting Guidelines for Evidence‐Based Practice. Worldviews on Evidence-Based Nursing, 14(6), 463–472. https://doi.org/10.1111/wvn.12258
caption: It is easy to mix up the tools used to evaluate literature and the tools used to write papers. Understanding this distinction is fundamental for evidence-based practice. Which tool do you use most frequently in your journal clubs?

title: Why Opaque Reporting Sabotages Research

slides.heading: The Danger of Opaque Reporting
slides.body: Opaque reporting is directly associated with biased conclusions and errors in biomedical publishing.
slides.image_prompt: a stack of heavy medical journals covered by a dark cloth with a question mark printed on top

slides.heading: Judging Reliability Becomes Impossible
slides.body: Without a clear understanding of how a study was done, readers are unable to judge whether the findings are reliable.
slides.image_prompt: a person holding two puzzle pieces that do not fit together over an open research paper

takeaway: Without clear methodological details, readers cannot judge if study findings are reliable.
references: Moher, D., Altman, D. G., Schulz, K. F., Simera, I., & Wager, E. (2014). Guidelines for reporting health research: A user’s manual.

Buccheri, R. K., & Sharifi, C. (2017). Critical Appraisal Tools and Reporting Guidelines for Evidence‐Based Practice. Worldviews on Evidence-Based Nursing, 14(6), 463–472. https://doi.org/10.1111/wvn.12258
caption: Poor reporting wastes scarce resources and leads to flawed clinical decisions. Transparency in methodology is non-negotiable. Have you ever encountered a published paper missing critical procedural details?
source_hint: Rationale for Using Reporting Guidelines in Publishing

title: Why the Barthel Index Misses Stroke Recovery

slides.heading: The Ceiling Effect Problem
slides.body: Many outcome measures in neurological rehabilitation suffer from floor or ceiling effects, which limit the ability to pick up change over time.
slides.image_prompt: a group of simple figures trying to jump and hitting an invisible low ceiling above them, with one figure holding a clipboard

slides.heading: High Scores, Residual Deficits
slides.body: Individuals may achieve high scores on the Barthel index but have residual deficits in gait, upper extremity recovery, driving, and physical functioning.
slides.image_prompt: a patient holding a high scoring grade document while stumbling with a cane and dropping car keys

slides.heading: Insensitive to Change
slides.body: The Barthel index has a ceiling effect and will not be sensitive to important clinical changes in stroke recovery.
slides.image_prompt: a measuring scale with a pointer stuck at the maximum top position while a patient walks past with difficulty

takeaway: Scales with ceiling effects fail to detect vital clinical changes in stroke recovery.
references: Balu, S. (2009). Differences in psychometric properties, cut-off scores, and outcomes between the Barthel Index and Modified Rankin Scale in pharmacotherapy-based stroke trials: systematic literature review. Current Medical Research and Opinion, 25(6), 1329–1341. https://doi.org/10.1185/03007990902875877
Hobart, J. C., Lamping, D. L., Freeman, J. A., Thompson, A. J., & Hobart, J. C. (2001). Evidence-based measurement: which disability scale for neurologic rehabilitation?
caption: Choosing outcome measures in neurological research is fraught with hidden traps. When an assessment tool like the Barthel index hits a ceiling, patients with lingering impairments in mobility or arm function look completely recovered on paper. How do you account for hidden functional deficits in your clinical trials?

title: Why Proxy Assessors Bias Quality of Life Data

slides.heading: Who Answers the Questionnaire?
slides.body: Assessments may be performed by rehabilitation providers, patients, or proxies, but each respondent type introduces unique rating discrepancies.
slides.image_prompt: three simple figures representing a doctor, a patient, and a relative holding different rating documents and pointing in separate directions

slides.heading: Proxies Overestimate Disability
slides.body: Proxy assessors tend to assess patients as more disabled than they appear on other measures of functional disability, especially in impaired patients.
slides.image_prompt: a relative looking at a patient through a magnifying glass and writing down a much larger disability score on a pad

slides.heading: The Frame of Reference Trap
slides.body: Healthcare professionals tend to rate patients higher than patients rate themselves due to a difference in the frame of reference used.
slides.image_prompt: a doctor and a patient looking at a staircase through two completely different colored glasses

takeaway: Proxy and provider reporting biases heavily distort patient functional and quality of life outcomes.
references: Duncan, P. W., Lai, S. M., Tyler, D., Perera, S., Reker, D. M., & Studenski, S. (2002). Evaluation of Proxy Responses to the Stroke Impact Scale. Stroke, 33(11), 2593–2599. https://doi.org/10.1161/01.str.0000034395.06874.3e

Sneeuw, K. C., Sprangers, M. A., & Aaronson, N. K. (2002). The role of health care providers and significant others in evaluating the quality of life of patients with chronic disease. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 55(11), 1130–1143. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0895-4356(02)00479-1

Williams, L. S., Bakas, T., Brizendine, E., Plue, L., Tu, W., Hendrie, H., & Kroenke, K. (2006). How Valid Are Family Proxy Assessments of Stroke Patients’ Health-Related Quality of Life?. Stroke, 37(8), 2081–2085. https://doi.org/10.1161/01.str.0000230583.10311.9f
caption: When patients cannot self-report due to cognitive or communication barriers, researchers often turn to proxy respondents or clinicians. However, studies show that family members view patients as significantly more disabled, while clinicians use entirely different reference norms. How do you handle respondent discrepancies in your studies?

title: Why the Mini-Mental State Exam Misses Stroke Deficits

slides.heading: The Limitations of the MMSE
slides.body: The most widely used cognitive screen is the Mini-Mental Status Exam, but this measure does not adequately represent executive function.
slides.image_prompt: a simple figure looking at a brain puzzle with a missing central piece labeled executive function while holding a clipboard

slides.heading: Missing Cognitive Impairment
slides.body: Due to its structural limitations, the traditional Mini-Mental Status Exam often misses significant cognitive impairment in neurological patients.
slides.image_prompt: a magnifying glass scanning a cognitive test paper and highlighting a blank overlooked section

slides.heading: Harmonizing Standards
slides.body: Expert groups have convened to recommend robust minimum clinical standards for the description and study of vascular cognitive impairment.
slides.image_prompt: a group of simple figures sitting around a table reviewing standardized neurological testing documents

takeaway: Relying solely on the MMSE risks missing vital executive and cognitive deficits in clinical research.
references: Folstein, M. F., Folstein, S. E., & McHugh, P. R. (1975). "Mini-mental state": A practical method for grading the cognitive state of patients for the clinician.

Hachinski, V., Iadecola, C., Petersen, R. C., Breteler, M. M., Nyenhuis, D. L., Black, S. E., ... & Winblad, B. (2006). National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke-Canadian Stroke Network vascular cognitive impairment harmonization standards.

Pendlebury, S. T., Cuthbertson, F. C., Welch, S. J., Mehta, Z., & Rothwell, P. M. (2010). Underestimation of Cognitive Impairment by Mini-Mental State Examination Versus the Montreal Cognitive Assessment in Patients With Transient Ischemic Attack and Stroke. Stroke, 41(6), 1290–1293. https://doi.org/10.1161/strokeaha.110.579888
caption: Cognitive assessment in neurological research is notoriously tricky. While the MMSE is a ubiquitous screening tool, it lacks adequate representation for executive function, leading researchers to miss subtle yet critical cognitive deficits. What cognitive screening tools do you rely on in your protocols?

title: Why Even One Outlier Destroys the Mean

slides.heading: The Mean Has Zero Breakdown
slides.body: The sample mean is defined as the sum of observations divided by n. If any single observation gets arbitrarily large, the mean becomes arbitrarily large. Thus the breakdown point for the mean is 0.
slides.image_prompt: a single towering bar chart column towering over smaller columns, pulling a heavy horizontal line upward with a tight rope, while simple figures watch in confusion

slides.heading: The Median Survives Extremes
slides.body: The median is the central value in a distribution where equal numbers of values lie above and below. If a minority of observations go to infinity, the median will not be arbitrarily bad. Its breakdown point is one half.
slides.image_prompt: a balance scale with multiple identical figures on one side and one giant figure on the other side, remaining perfectly level with a bright dividing line in the middle

slides.heading: When Is the Mean Actually Good?
slides.body: From the point of robustness and breakdown point, the mean is a good estimator only if the data have zero outliers, no skewness, and unimodality. The median is far more insensitive to these departures from normality.
slides.image_prompt: a magnifying glass inspecting a pristine bell shaped curve document, while three distorted bumpy documents are tossed aside into a waste bin

takeaway: Even a single outlier makes the sample mean completely arbitrary, giving it a breakdown point of zero.
references: Donoho, D., & Huber, P. (Eds.). (1983). The notion of breakdown point.
caption: In biomedical datasets, outliers and skewness are extremely common. Yet we often default to the sample mean without checking if our data meet the strict assumptions of normality. When a single extreme value can drag our entire estimate off course, relying solely on parametric measures becomes a risky gamble. How often do you check for breakdown points before choosing your primary summary statistic?

title: Parametric vs Nonparametric: The Cost of Power

slides.heading: Asymptotic Relative Efficiency
slides.body: Asymptotic Relative Efficiency defines how many more subjects are needed for a nonparametric test to have equivalent power as a parametric test for a fixed Type I error rate.
slides.image_prompt: two parallel lines of simple figures of different lengths, with a researcher holding a measuring tape and counting groups of people at a wooden table

slides.heading: The Price of Using Nonparametric Tests
slides.body: The ARE of the Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test versus the t-test when underlying assumptions are satisfied is zero point nine five five. There is minimal power loss when data are normal.
slides.image_prompt: a simple weighing scale holding two almost identical pill bottles, showing a minuscule difference between the two pans under a bright desk lamp

slides.heading: Massive Gains When Normality Fails
slides.body: Nonparametric tests are much more powerful than their parametric counterparts when underlying distributions are heavy tailed or have extreme skewness. In some cases ARE became infinite.
slides.image_prompt: a crowded room of simple figures separating into two contrasting paths, guided by a large glowing arrow pointing toward a robust shielded container

takeaway: Using nonparametric tests when data are normal results in minimal power loss, but brings massive power gains when normality fails.
references: Hodges, J. L., & Lehmann, E. L. (1956). The Efficiency of Some Nonparametric Competitors of the $t$-Test. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 27(2), 324–335. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177728261
Chernoff, H., & Savage, I. (1958). Asymptotic normality and efficiency of certain nonparametric tests. Ann Math Stat, 29, 927-999.
caption: Choosing between parametric and nonparametric tests often sparks heated debates among researchers. While t-tests are the gold standard for normal distributions, real-world biomedical data rarely cooperate. Knowing the Asymptotic Relative Efficiency helps us weigh the small cost of nonparametrics against their massive protection against skewed data. Have you ever swapped a t-test for a Wilcoxon test mid-analysis?

title: Why Nonparametric Tests Shine in Small Samples

slides.heading: The Small Sample Reality
slides.body: Because of cost and potential risks to humans and animals, many sample sizes in the biomedical literature are far from infinite, often remaining under twenty-five per group.
slides.image_prompt: a small group of twenty five simple figures standing inside a fenced enclosure next to a large budget document marked with warning symbols

slides.heading: WRST in Small Samples
slides.body: Monte Carlo experiments found that for tests of location shift, the Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test was the best test in almost all cases, matching or exceeding t-test power.
slides.image_prompt: a researcher examining small sample containers through a magnifying glass while sorting them into two neat rows on a wooden workbench

slides.heading: Handling Non-Normality in Small Trials
slides.body: Under extreme asymmetry or point mass distributions, nonparametric tests demonstrated large power advantages over the t-test even with small sample sizes.
slides.image_prompt: a split group of simple figures stepping over uneven terrain toward two distinct markers, guided by bold directional arrows

takeaway: In small samples with non-normal data, nonparametric tests offer remarkable power advantages over parametric alternatives.
references: Tanizaki, H. (1997). Power comparison of nonparametric tests: small sample properties from Monte Carol experiments. J Appl Stat, 24, 603-632.
Bridge, P., & Sawilowsky, S. (1999). Increasing physicians’ awareness of the impact of statistics on research outcomes. J Clin Epidemiol, 52, 229-235.
caption: Small sample sizes are a persistent challenge in clinical research, driven by ethical constraints and high costs. When data violate normality assumptions in these tight cohorts, standard parametric tests can mislead us. Fortunately, evidence from Monte Carlo studies shows nonparametric alternatives maintain robust performance. How do you handle small, skewed cohorts in your studies?
